**On Things That Move Too Slowly to See**

There is a kind of motion that hides in plain sight. Not the motion of a bird crossing a window or a leaf letting go of its branch, but the motion of the branch itself, thickening by a fraction of a millimeter each year. The motion of the hour hand. The motion of the coastline, giving up a few inches to the sea while nobody is paying attention. I find myself drawn to this category of things, the ones that are unquestionably moving and yet appear, to any observer with ordinary patience, to be perfectly still.

Take the moon. Every year it drifts about three and a half centimeters farther from Earth, roughly the rate at which a fingernail grows. It has been doing this for billions of years. The reason is a kind of slow gravitational conversation: the moon pulls on our oceans, raising tides, and the tides drag against the spinning Earth, and the energy has to go somewhere, so it goes into lifting the moon into a slightly higher orbit. In exchange, the Earth's rotation slows. Our days are getting longer, about two milliseconds per century. When the dinosaurs lived, a day was closer to twenty-three hours. Long before that, in the Precambrian, it may have been eighteen. Somewhere in the deep past the moon hung enormous in the sky, close enough that tides were violent things, sweeping far inland twice a day.

None of this is visible. You could stare at the moon your entire life and never see it retreat. And yet the retreat is as real as anything you can touch. The fact that a thing is imperceptible says nothing about whether it is happening.

Stalactites grow at a rate of perhaps a tenth of a millimeter a year, each drop of mineral-laden water leaving behind a whisper of calcite before falling. A stalactite the length of your arm might be older than agriculture. Cave explorers are told never to touch them, not because they are fragile in the ordinary sense but because the oils on a human hand can halt growth that has been proceeding uninterrupted for ten thousand years. There is something almost unbearable about that: that a formation older than every city on Earth can be stopped by a moment of careless curiosity.

Continents move at about the speed fingernails grow, too. This comparison gets used so often it has become a cliché, but I think it stays in circulation because it does real work. It takes something inconceivable and puts it in the register of the body. The Atlantic Ocean widens by roughly the width of a thumb each year. Over a human lifetime that adds up to about the length of a car. Over the lifetime of the species it adds up to the distance you might walk before breakfast. And over the two hundred million years since the Atlantic began to open, it adds up to an ocean.

I think what compels me about these slow motions is that they force a reckoning with the limits of perception as a guide to truth. We are built to notice things that happen on the timescale of a heartbeat, a breath, a season. A predator moves fast; fruit ripens over weeks; winter comes once a year. Our attention was tuned by what mattered for survival, and what mattered for survival happened quickly. The result is that we walk around with an instinctive sense that what appears still is still, and that sense is simply wrong about almost everything.

Consider a tree. A mature oak might add a ring each year, a sleeve of new wood wrapped around all the old ones. You can stand beside it every day and never see it change. But come back after a decade and the branch that once brushed your shoulder now clears your head. The tree did not grow while you were away; it was growing the whole time, in front of you, and you could not see it. This is not a failure of eyesight. It is a mismatch of clocks.

Language moves this way, too. No one alive watched "nice" shift from meaning foolish to meaning pleasant, or "silly" from blessed to ridiculous. These changes took centuries, and every speaker along the way felt they were using the word correctly, because they were. The drift happened in the space between generations, in the small mishearings and playful extensions that each person makes without noticing. Read a letter from three hundred years ago and the accumulated motion is suddenly visible, the way a time-lapse film reveals the frantic life of a plant that seemed inert.

And of course we ourselves are the clearest case. The face in the mirror looks the same as yesterday, and the same as the day before. It is only the old photograph, dragged out of a drawer, that reveals how far the coastline has retreated. Aging is continental drift on a human body, imperceptible in any given moment and undeniable in aggregate. We are not the same people we were, and we never caught ourselves changing.

I do not find this bleak. If anything it feels like a corrective to a certain impatience. So much of life is spent waiting for visible results, for the moment when effort produces something you can point to. But most of the important processes in the world do not work on that schedule. The cave is being built. The ocean is opening. The tree is climbing toward the light at a pace that mocks the calendar. If these things can proceed without applause, without even being seen, perhaps the slow work of a life can too. Perhaps the fact that nothing seems to be happening is not evidence that nothing is.

Somewhere above the rooftops tonight the moon is a few centimeters farther than it was last year. Tomorrow will be two milliseconds longer than a day in Julius Caesar's Rome. Nobody will notice. It is happening anyway.
